policies.summary: Municipal zoning bylaws may not regulate generation, storage or transmission facilities reviewed under section 248; towns keep only solar screening rules (which the Commission applies unless they would effectively prohibit the facility) and substantial deference to energy-compliant town and regional plans.

No company or person may begin site preparation or construction of an in-state electric generation or energy storage facility (other than one used solely for the owner's on-site consumption) without a certificate of public good from the Public Utility Commission, which must give due consideration to municipal and regional recommendations.

Ground-mounted solar facilities approved under section 248 must be set back at least 100 feet from state or town highways and 50 feet from other property lines when larger than 150 kW (smaller tiers for smaller plants); the Commission may require more, or accept less by agreement with the town and adjoining owners.

projects.description: Allco Renewable Energy’s plans for the 2-MW Apple Hill project and 2-MW Willow Road project in Bennington, Vermont have faced opposition from neighbors for close to a decade.
In July 2017, the Vermont Public Utility Commission rejected an application for a certificate of public good for the Kidder Hill Wind project.

Several individuals joined with Energize Vermont in filing a lawsuit to challenge the issuance of a permit related to stormwater management at the 21-turbine Kingdom Community Wind Project, which was completed in 2012.
In September 2021, the Vermont Public Utility Commission denied a certificate to a 500-kilowatt project in Manchester, Vermont, which had been proposed by Manchester-based MHG Solar.

On March 30, 2018, the developer of a proposed 2.2-MW solar project near downtown Brandon wrote a letter to the Vermont Public Utility Commission requesting permission to change the site of the project because of “significant opposition to the project from neighboring property owners and residents due to aesthetic concerns.”
In July 2016, AllEarth Renewables proposed a single 2.2-MW wind turbine on a 450-acre dairy air farm in the Town of Holland, after winning a state contract.
In 2022, the developer of a proposed single-turbine, 1.5-MW wind project abandoned plans amidst opposition in Castleton, Vermont and surrounding towns.
In 2017, the Vermont Supreme Court rejected a nuisance lawsuit by neighbors of two solar projects in New Haven, alleging that the projects had caused their properties to lose value.
The 85-acre, 20-MW Shaftsbury Solar project, proposed by Freepoint Commodities and SunEast Development LLC, has faced significant opposition in Bennington County.
In December 2023, Norwich Solar abandoned plans for a 2.2-MW, 500-foot turbine in Stamford, Vermont, which would have been the first utility-scale wind project in the state.
In November 2016, the towns of Windham and Grafton both decided by non-binding referendum votes to reject the Stiles Brooks Wind Project.
In late 2015, the towns of Swanton and Fairfield both voted to oppose the Swanton Wind Farm.
A proposal to build the Viridis solar farm, a 300-acre, 50-MW project in the Town of Panton, has faced significant opposition from local residents.
